en: A Concise Commentary on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, composed by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Peng Jiqing.
In explaining this sūtra, I shall briefly open it into four sections: first, elucidating the essential points within the sūtra; second, elucidating the benefits of rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Third, the specific presentation of questions and answers; fourth, the recitation of verses for dedication.

This sutra takes the single mind as its core principle, the upholding of the name as its practice, faith and aspiration as its guide, non-retrogression as its path, and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as its ultimate goal. How, then, does one cultivate this single mind?
This is established as the fundamental tenet: this single mind alone is the source of all Buddhas and the life-force of wisdom for all sentient beings.

Because of delusion, one wanders through the three realms of suffering; because of awakening, one directly ascends to the other shore. Although delusion and awakening differ, they are fundamentally unmoving from the beginning.

Simply by being free from the deluded perceptions of external objects, the radiance becomes brilliantly clear, pervading the entire *sahasra-lokadhātu* and continuing without interruption until the end of the future.
Therefore, it is called "Immeasurable Light" (*Amitābha*) and also called "Immeasurable Life" (*Amitāyus*).
Thus, one should know that this immeasurable light and life are not separate from sentient beings at any time; they are present where deliberation cannot reach and where one cannot grasp them.

The point of attachment is simply that people fail to see it before their very eyes. Our Śākyamuni Buddha, through his compassionate skillful means, pointed toward the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and universally exhorted beings to be reborn there.
He elucidated the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation, taking "single-mindedness without distraction" as its core.

As it is said: "If one restrains the mind to a single point, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. When recitation reaches its ultimate limit, deluded emotions are emptied, and the fundamental light manifests of itself.

How is it that "holding" (dhāraṇī) is called "practice"? The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "By virtue of reciting the Buddha’s name, in every thought-moment, one eliminates the offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death.
This is because the name summons the virtues; the three bodies—the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body—are fully encompassed therein without exception.

Thus, the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā Sūtra* specifically designates "holding the name" as the "One-Practice Samādhi. However, these sentient beings have, from time immemorial, been bound by their habitual afflictions...
It is like oil entering flour; unless one arouses a courageous mind and initiates diligent practice, but instead remains indolent and complacent, how could one ever gain entry?
Therefore, one must set a fixed period to achieve results, from one day up to seven days, until one inevitably reaches single-mindedness before ceasing.
Once this single-mindedness is attained, the Buddha is no different from the mind, and the mind is no different from the Buddha. Whether sitting, lying down, or walking, [one remains thus].

When all other thoughts are extinguished, the purity of the Buddha-land follows the purity of one’s own mind; thus, transforming the Sahā world into Sukhāvatī depends solely upon the individual and is not beyond their reach.
How then can faith and aspiration serve as the guide? As the Sūtra says:

"You should all believe and accept my words, as well as what has been spoken by all the Buddhas. Regarding "faith," there is faith in the three periods of time and faith in the existence of the Western Pure Land.

If one believes that reciting the Buddha’s name for even a single thought-moment will certainly lead to seeing the Buddha, and because of seeing the Buddha, one will certainly attain Buddhahood—this is called faith based on the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature).

Faith based on the *paratantra-svabhāva* is weak in power. One must believe that the three periods of time are not separate from one's own mind, and that one's own mind is fully endowed with the Western Pure Land.
One must believe that reciting the Buddha’s name for a single thought-moment is itself the Buddha; to recite the Buddha’s name in every thought-moment is... [no further text provided].
When one does not think of the Buddha, and so forth, until one is detached from both the "is" and the "is-not," one suddenly perceives the ground of True Suchness and tranquil extinction.
This is called right faith; it is also called pure faith; it is also called complete faith. As the Sūtra says: "Sentient beings who hear this should make a vow."

"I vow to be born in that land. As for this vow: "I vow that I may leave suffering and attain happiness; I vow that I may abandon defilement and attain purity"—this is the cause of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Their vows are narrow. [In contrast,] one should only give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi, desiring to universally cause all sentient beings to leave suffering and attain happiness, and desiring to universally cause all sentient beings to abandon defilement and take up purity. This is...
Therefore, although they are born in the Pure Land, they do not abandon Saṃsāra; although they dwell in Saṃsāra, they vow to be born together with all sentient beings in Sukhāvatī.
This is called the Right Vow, the Great Vow, and the Unsurpassed Vow. To possess such faith—
One who makes such a vow is able to enter deeply through a single gate onto the path of wondrous adornment.
How does one take non-retrogression as the standard? A sutra states: "All sentient beings who are born [in this land] are *avaivartika*. *Avaivartika* is translated here as "non-retrogressive.
In this land, there are many obstacles and difficulties; even Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas may remain dimly aware of their past causes and forget their original nature.

How much more so for ordinary beings who plant small roots of goodness; when their retribution is exhausted, they fall back again. Without relying on the power of the Buddha, it is difficult to perfect the supreme fruit.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva reflects thus: 'I have not yet attained the Buddha-eye; I am no different from one who is blind.'"
If they are not guided by the Buddha, they will have no destination and will mistakenly enter other paths.

Even if they hear the Buddha’s Dharma, those who practice in different places do not know the proper timing for instruction or the extent of the practices to be performed. When a bodhisattva sees the Buddha—whether seeing him with their eyes—
With a pure mind, if one hears what is taught, the mind will delight in the Dharma, attain great wisdom, and by practicing in accordance with the Dharma, achieve liberation.
Since such benefits from encountering a Buddha are immeasurable, how could one not single-mindedly seek to see the Buddha?
Furthermore, it is said: "Bodhisattvas do not prize the worldly bliss and merit of a *cakravartin* king or of humans and devas;

they simply keep the Buddhas in mind and constantly cultivate the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. Therefore, wherever they are born, they always encounter the Buddhas. Thus we know that those who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment] and wish to definitely attain Buddhahood must never be separated from the Buddhas.
To be unseparated from the Buddhas, one must first practice the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states: "There is no..."
Amitāyus Buddha possesses eighty-four thousand marks; each mark has eighty-four thousand secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*);

each secondary characteristic has eighty-four thousand rays of light; and each ray of light shines everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions, embracing and never abandoning those sentient beings who mindfully recite his name.
Thus we know that the Buddha’s light is like a mirror, and sentient beings are like reflections. The body facing the mirror—
No shadow fails to appear. Thus, the Sūtra says: "All these people shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Within the Great Radiance, there is absolutely no cause for regression.
Why, then, is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* considered the ultimate? [It is] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This is called Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas claim to have already realized nirvāṇa and never aspire for the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, they neither hear nor see the immeasurable sounds of Dharma or the boundless Buddha-activities.
This is because they have not generated the bodhicitta, nor have they caused others to abide in the bodhicitta. Thus says the Buddha.

For forty-nine years, he preached the Dharma, employing various skillful means to refine and purify his disciples. It was only at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that he finally exhausted his original intent, revealing the provisional to manifest the ultimate.
All the great disciples were then granted predictions of their future enlightenment. This was solely because this Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle is difficult to speak of and difficult to understand.
Thus, while the youth Sudhana had already resolved upon the Great Mind and traveled extensively to visit spiritual friends, [the Buddha] passed away.
Samantabhadra leads beings back to Sukhāvatī by means of the ten great kings of vows, desiring that they may fulfill the practices and vows of Samantabhadra and ultimately attain Buddhahood.
Now, through the causes and conditions of mindfulness of the Buddha, one resolves to see the Buddha; because of seeing the Buddha, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Compared to those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who linger at the illusory city, the difference between their days and kalpas is such that the former cannot even be measured against the latter.
This is the analogy of the clouds. Thus, one knows that this sutra is both sudden and perfect;
it directly elucidates and illuminates the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* because they are ultimately and completely without distinction.

Only when one clearly understands the ultimate intent is one said to receive and uphold this sutra, to believe and accept what all Buddhas have taught, and to make offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, thereby accomplishing wisdom.
The body does not depend on another for awakening; it is fundamentally non-moving from the beginning—how could there be any falling back?
The above concludes the explanation of the essential points of this sutra. Next, the benefits of rebirth shall now be explained.

Regarding the fact that there are no various sufferings in that Buddha-land, briefly stated, there are four matters. First, there is no suffering of the womb or the hells, because one takes up a physical form within a lotus flower. First.

There is no suffering of aging, illness, death, or decline, because their lifespan is immeasurable. First, there is no suffering of obstruction from the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), because they travel at will to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
Second, they do not undergo the suffering of saṃsāra, because the three evil realms do not exist there.

Next, to clarify that they experience only various forms of bliss, it is briefly stated that there are six matters: first, the faculty of the eye is pure, because it is radiant with the light of various jewels.
First, the faculty of hearing is purified, because all dharmas flow forth and are proclaimed. Second, the faculty of the tongue is purified, because it is satiated with supreme flavors.
First, the faculty of the nose is purified because fragrant flowers cover the ground. Second, the faculty of the body is purified because one bathes the body with the eight waters.
Third, the faculty of the mind is purified because one constantly recollects the Triple Gem. For those born in that land, there are five further matters by which it excels other Buddha-lands:
first, Amitābha Buddha is always present preaching the Dharma; second, the transformation bodies of Amitābha Buddha are without limit...
Because of these measures: first, because the light of Amitābha Buddha shines everywhere; second, because all superior and virtuous people assemble in one place;
and third, because the Buddhas of the ten directions protect and keep them in mind with one heart. Such a Dharma as this is difficult to hear.

To hear this and believe it is the most difficult of difficulties. This is because within the five turbidities of this evil world, there is only manifold suffering and not a single thing to be enjoyed;

furthermore, one is born during the age of the final dharma, where one does not see the Buddhas and does not hear them preach the Dharma. Those who encounter this sutra should give rise to a sense of preciousness and the thought that it is difficult to meet.

By practicing according to what is taught, they will achieve completion in a single lifetime. This is [the mark of]... [not... (Note: The final phrase "This is not" appears to be an incomplete fragment in the source text.)
This fulfills the intent of our Buddha’s teaching of the sutras and the guidance of the protective mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
it is a great karmic opportunity for transforming from the ordinary to the sagely throughout a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas. How can one not exert oneself?

The above concludes the explanation of the benefits of rebirth. A separate series of questions and answers follows, consisting of approximately four sections, intended to resolve various doubts and to strengthen the faith of the assembly.
Question: Within the pure mind, there is originally not a single thing. How then can there be such merits and such adornments?

"How is this different from pressing on the eyes to see flowers, or drawing circles on the ground to make cakes? [The questioner asks. [The Master] answers: "That which is fundamentally without a single thing refers to the fact that phenomena themselves are without marks;
it does not mean that everything is annihilated. The Sixth Patriarch said: "The world and empty space can contain the forms and images of the myriad things."
The sun, moon, and stars; mountains, rivers, and the great earth; springs, sources, streams, and ravines; grasses, trees, and forests; evil people and virtuous people;
unwholesome dharmas and wholesome dharmas; heavens and hells; all the great oceans and Mount Sumerus—all these are contained within space.
The emptiness of the nature of sentient beings is likewise so. Therefore, know that once the emptiness of nature is fully realized, all forms and appearances are empty;
their adornment with merit is like flowers in a mirror or the moon in water. Failing to realize the emptiness of nature, one may loathe clamor and seek stillness;

even if such a person can partially realize nirvana, they are merely a dull-witted arhat. Question: When suffering and pleasure are both forgotten, and purity and impurity are non-dual, [what remains?]
Only then does one accord with True Suchness (*tathatā*). How, then, could there be such fervent grasping and rejecting within it? Answer:

The waterfowl, trees, forests, jewel ponds, and pearl nets are accomplished through the pure vows of the Buddhas; the hills, mounds, ravines, pits, tiles, rubble, thorns, and briars are evoked by the defiled karma of sentient beings.

The wise understand that these are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), yet because they still possess the adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) from beginningless time, they must rely upon purity.

Conditioned by this, one counteracts residual habits; through seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), and only then is one capable of delivering sentient beings according to their various types.

To remain on the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) while failing to seek liberation, yet falsely hoping for the realization of a sage—such a thing is impossible. Question: At the time of death...
Amitābha Buddha appears before one. Is this his manifested emanations responding universally to beings, or is it merely what is manifested by consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*)?
If it is "merely consciousness," then these are illusions and not real. If it is "emanated bodies," then apart from the mind there is no Buddha.

Answer: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm; he appears universally before all sentient beings. Responding to conditions and meeting with those who feel [the need], there is nothing that is not reached."
It is not limited, yet it eternally dwells upon this seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Because it manifests universally, it may be described as having emanated bodies;
because it accords with conditions, it is also established as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Thus, the Elder Vimokṣaka said: "Those Tathāgatas do not come here, and my body does not go there.
There is neither coming nor going, yet coming and going are perfectly manifest. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is perfectly interfused."

This is inconceivable. Question: The Sixth Patriarch said that when people of the East recite the Buddha’s name, they seek rebirth in the West; when people of the West recite the Buddha’s name, in which land do they seek rebirth?
Ordinary, ignorant people do not understand their own nature and do not recognize the pure land within their own bodies;

thus they long for the East or the West. For those who have attained awakening, it is the same wherever they are. These words of the ancient masters are true—how could one not believe them? Answer: This is merely for the duration of a single period.

Discourse regarding the "sweeping away" [of delusions] does not yet accord with the perfect teaching. As for those in the Western Land who are reborn in various realms: by reciting the Buddha’s name while dwelling in the realm of common residence (*sābhoga*), one is born in the land of expedient means (*upāya-bhūmi*);

by reciting the Buddha’s name while in the land of expedient means, one is born in the land of true recompense (*vipāka-bhūmi*); and by reciting the Buddha’s name while in the land of true recompense, one is born in the land of tranquil light (*śāntaprabhā-bhūmi*).

Thus, we know that the single Dharma-gate of reciting the Buddha’s name vertically encompasses the four lands. For one who has realized the fundamental source, even the seeking of the mind is impossible.
It is so. How could one seek a pure land apart from within this illusory body?
If one realizes that this "unobtainable mind" pervades all places, then to be reborn there by the power of one's vows is like space sealing space—what hindrance could there be?
The preceding detailed exposition of questions and answers is concluded. It is followed by these verses for universal recitation and dedication with single-minded devotion:
How excellent is Śākyamuni, Who manifests in this world of five turbidities To preach this Dharma so difficult to believe, Which cuts across the current of birth and death!
How excellent is Amitāyus, Whose land is wondrously adorned!
Universally emitting great radiance, he gathers in boundless multitudes;
Those who hear his name and are able to uphold it will certainly be born in that land, Spontaneously attaining the stage of non-retrogression and realizing unsurpassed bodhi.
Whether on Vulture Peak or in royal palaces, he universally exhorts all to be born in the Pure Land; This [teaching] is now present here in the Jeta Grove.
To speak of my own accord without being asked is truly due to great compassion, like rescuing those from fire or saving those drowning in water.
How could one who hears this Dharma not conceive a sense of its rarity? For how long kalpas have they endured saṃsāra;
by what means can they attain liberation? Now, relying upon the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), I shall expound and elucidate the sūtras.
The Bhagavāns of the ten directions—these are made solely by this one mind.
If one attains Buddhahood simply by recollecting the Buddha, how is this different from the relationship between a shadow and its form? I universally exhort all sons of the Buddha:
believe these words of truth, and practice diligently according to what has been taught. Like lamps passing the flame to one another, this is the most supreme of golden platforms.
Taking birth therein, they return once more to deliver sentient beings, ultimately attaining the Way of Buddhahood.
*The A-mi-t'o Sūtra: An Abridged Treatise* (End).
